name: Palladas of Alexandria
bio: Palladas of Alexandria was a grammarian and the last great epigrammatist of pagan Alexandria, known for bitter, satirical verse. The editor dates him to the fourth century AD; Paton's index says the fifth.
The epigrams here are those that Paton's first volume ascribes to him.

poems.title: Book V, 71
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Zenon, since you have married the daughter of Protomachus (first in fight) and of Nicomache (conquering in fight) you have war in your house. Search for a kind seducer, a Lysimachus (deliverer from fight) who will take pity on you and deliver you from Andromache (husband-fighter) the daughter of Protomachus.

poems.title: Book V, 72
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: This is life, and nothing else is; life is delight ; away, dull care! Brief are the years of man. To-day wine is ours, and the dance, and flowery wreaths, and women. To-day let me live well; none knows what may be to-morrow.

poems.title: Book V, 257
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Now I condemn Zeus as a tepid lover, since he did not transform himself for this haughty fair’s sake. She is not second in beauty to Europa or Danae or tender Leda. But perhaps he disdains courtesans, for know they were maiden princesses he used to seduce.

poems.title: Book VI, 60
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Pamphile, in place of an ox and a golden offering, dedicated to Isis these glossy locks ; and the goddess takes more pleasure in them than Apollo in the gold that Croesus sent him from Lydia.

poems.title: Book VI, 61
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: O heavenly razor, happy razor with which Pamphile shore her plaited tresses to dedicate them. It was no human smith that wrought thee, but beside the forge of Hephaestus the bright-snooded Grace (to use Homer’s words) took up the golden hammer and fashioned thee with her own hands.

poems.title: Book VI, 85
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: His breaster and leggers and shield and spear and heller Captain Gordy dedicates to Timothy.

poems.title: Book VII, 607
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Old Psyllo, grudging her heirs, made herself her own heir and with a quick leap went down to the house of Hades, contriving to end her life and her outlay at the same time. Having eaten up all her fortune, she perished together with her spending power, and jumped to Hades when her last penny was gone.

poems.title: Book VII, 610
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: One carried off a bride and Fate carried off the wedding party, despoiling of life the merry company. One wedding sent four and twenty corpses to their graves, and one chamber became their common mortuary. Penthesilea, unhappy bride, Pentheus bridegroom of sorrow, rich in deaths was your marriage!

poems.title: Book VII, 681
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: You did not go abroad for the sake of honour, but of death, and although lame you ran to Hades, Gessius, swifter than the Fates. For you retreated from life owing to the advancement of which you were dreaming.

poems.title: Book VII, 682
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Gessius did not die hurried by Fate, but arrived in Hades before Fate.

poems.title: Book VII, 683
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: The wisest of the Seven Sages said “Naught in excess,” but you, Gessius, were not convinced of it, and came to this end. Though erudite, you incurred the reproach of the greatest lack of reason in desiring to ascend to heaven. Thus it was that Pegasus was fatal to Bellerophon, because he wished to learn the rules of motion of the stars. But he had a horse and the confident strength of youth, whereas Gessius could not screw his courage up enough even to ease himself.

poems.title: Book VII, 684
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Let no mortal even seek to be a god also, nor pursue the pride of high office. Gessius is the proof of it, for he was first of all puffed up and then collapsed, not content with mortal, felicity.

poems.title: Book VII, 685
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: You sought and found the end of life and happiness, seeking an office tending to the highest end. But you obtained the honour, Gessius, receiving after your death the insignia of office.

poems.title: Book VII, 686
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: When Baucalus saw Gessius just after his death, and lamer than ever, he spoke thus: “Gessius, what made thee descend into Hell, naked, without funeral, in new burial guise?” And to him in great wrath Gessius at once replied: “Baucalus, the pride of wealth may cause death.”

poems.title: Book VII, 687
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: When Gessius discovered the fraud of the oracle of Ammon not long before his death in a strange land, he blamed his own belief and that science, and those who trust in silly astrologers.

poems.title: Book VII, 688
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: The two soothsayers brought death on Gessius by their oaths, promising him the consular chair. O race of men vain minded, angry with themselves, knowing nothing even until the end of life.

poems.title: Book IX, 5
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: This pear-tree is the sweet result of the labour of my hand, with which in summer I fixed the graft in its moist bark. The slip, rooted on the tree by the incision, has changed its fruit, and though it is still a pyraster below, it is a fragrant-fruited pear-tree above.

poems.title: Book IX, 6
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: I was a pyraster; thy hand hath made me a fragrant pear-tree by inserting a graft, and I reward thee for thy kindness.

poems.title: Book IX, 119
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: If a man who is a ruler choose to put up with flatterers, he will sacrifice many to their vile mouths ; so the best men, in righteous hatred, should detest the flattered as much as the flatterer.

poems.title: Book IX, 165
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Woman is the wrath of Zeus, given to men in the place of fire, a grievous exchange. For she burns up and withers man with care, and brings hasty old age on youth. Even Zeus does not possess Hera of the golden throne unvexed; indeed he hath often cast her out from the immortals to hang in the mist and clouds; Homer knew this, and hath described even Zeus as being wrath with his wife. Thus never is a woman at concord with her husband, not even when she lies beside him on a floor of gold.

poems.title: Book IX, 166
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Homer shows us that every woman is wicked and treacherous; be she chaste or a whore, in either case she is perdition. Helen’s adultery caused the murder of men, and Penelope’s chastity caused death. All the woes of the Iliad were for the sake of one woman, and Penelope was the cause of the Odyssey.

poems.title: Book IX, 167
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Zeus, in place of fire, bestowed another fire, woman. Would that neither woman nor fire had come into being! Fire, it is true, is soon put out, but woman is a fire unquenchable, flaming, ever alight.

poems.title: Book IX, 169
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: The wrath of Achilles was the cause of pernicious poverty to me too, since I adopted the profession of a grammarian. Would that that “wrath” had killed me with the Greeks, before the bitter hunger of grammar had put an end to me. But all to let Agamemnon run away with Briseis, and Paris with Helen, I have become poor.

poems.title: Book IX, 170
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: I chastened my shameless belly by severe reasoning, correcting the troublesome gut by temperance. Indeed, if my intellect is in a higher place than my belly, how can I fail to subdue the inferior one of the two?

poems.title: Book IX, 171
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: I am selling the implements of the Muses, the books that have made me groan so much, now that I am taking to another profession. Farewell, ye Muses. I bid thee good-bye, Learning, for syntax is the death of me.

poems.title: Book IX, 172
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: I care no longer for either Hope or Fortune ; their deceit is now of no account to me; I have reached the haven. I am a poor man, but freedom is my house-mate, and I turn my back on wealth which insults poverty.

poems.title: Book IX, 173
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: The beginning of grammar ! is a curse in five lines. The first has the word “wrath,” the second “pernicious,” and after that “many woes” of the Greeks ; the third “leads down souls to Hades”; to the fourth belong “spoil” and “dogs”; to the fifth “birds” of ill-omen and the “anger of Zeus.” How, then, can a grammarian avoid having many sorrows after five curses and five cases (falls) ?

poems.title: Book IX, 174
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: The teachers here are those men with whom Sarapis is angry; they start from “pernicious wrath.” Here the nurse brings, perforce, the fee once a month, tying up the wretched pittance in byblus and paper, and puts the contemptible little paper, like a pinch of incense, by the master’s seat, as if by a tomb, She steals some of the small fee and changes the coins, substituting leaden ones, and she receives her commission, If any one agrees to pay a gold coin for a whole year, he changes his teacher in the eleventh month before paying up, and is so ungrateful as to make fun, too, of his former master after robbing him of a whole year’s fee.

poems.title: Book IX, 175
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: I sett Callimachus and Pindar, and all the cases in the grammar, being myself a sore case of poverty, For Dorotheus has cut off the salary that supported me, sending this impious message of complaint against me. But, dear Theo, protect me, and do not let me end my days in conjunction with poverty.

poems.title: Book IX, 176
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: I was invited to dinner by you, the orator, and if I failed to come I have the honour you paid me, and am still more your friend. For my heart does not rejoice in appreciation of viands, but is nourished only by the honour it tastes.

poems.title: Book IX, 180
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.note: Paton: This and the three following are written on the subject of a Temple of Fortune converted into a Tavern.
poems.text: Fortune, who pliest thy trade through all our life, whose nature is like untempered wine, thou who art ever mixing and pouring from vessel to vessel, now hast thou too become a tavern-keeper instead of a goddess, a calling suitable to thy character.

poems.title: Book IX, 181
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Times are turned topsy-turvy as I see, and we now see Fortune in misfortune.

poems.title: Book IX, 182
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: And thou, Lady Fortune, how has evil fortune befallen thee? How hast thou, who givest us good fortune, become unfortunate? Learn thou, too, to support thy own changes of tide, learn to suffer the unhappy falls which thou sendest to others.

poems.title: Book IX, 183
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: And of thee too, Fortune, they make mockery now thou art changed, and at the end thou hast not even spared thy own fortune. Thou who hadst once a temple, keepest a tavern in thy old age, and we see thee now serving hot drinks to mortals. Justly bewail thine own mischance, fickle goddess, now that thou reversest thine own fortune like that of mortals.

poems.title: Book IX, 377
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Tantalus ate nothing, for the fruit of the trees that tossed over his head ever eluded him, and owing to this, being in want of food, he was less thirsty ; but suppose he had eaten ripe figs, and plums, and apples, do dead men get so very thirsty from eating fresh fruit? But we guests eat all sorts of salted dishes, quails and cheese and goose’s fat, poultry and veal, and on the top of all drink only one glass. So we are worse off than you, Tantalus.

poems.title: Book IX, 378
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: They say that Sarapis appeared in a dream by night to a murderer who was sleeping under a decayed wall, and thus spoke as in an oracle: “Arise, thou who liest here, and seek, poor wretch, another sleeping place.” The man awoke and departed, and immediately the rotten wall fell to the ground. The evil-doer rejoiced, and in the morning sacrificed to the gods in thanks for his escape, thinking that Sarapis is pleased with murderers. But Sarapis appeared to him again at night, and prophesied thus to him: ‘“‘Wretch, dost thou think that I protect criminals? If I did not let thee be killed now, it is that thou now hast escaped a painless death; but know that thou art reserved for the cross.”

poems.title: Book IX, 379
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: The proverb says, “Even a pig would bite a bad man;” but I say that we should not say that, but “Even a pig would bite simple unmeddlesome men, but even a snake would be afraid to bite a bad man.”

poems.title: Book IX, 393
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: No magistrate ever came here who was both clean-handed and mild; for the one principle seems antagonistic to the other. Mildness is a virtue of the thief, and purity a virtue of the proud. These qualities are the two instruments of government.

poems.title: Book IX, 394
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: God, father of flatterers, son of pain and care, it is fear to have thee and pain not to have thee.

poems.title: Book IX, 395
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Odysseus said “nothing is sweeter than a man’s fatherland,” for in Circe’s isle he never ate cheese-cake. If he had seen even the smoke curling up from that, he would have sent ten Penelopes to the deuce.

poems.title: Book IX, 397
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: A Spartan once was flying from the battle, and his mother, uplifting a sword to smite his breast, exclaimed: “If thou livest, thou dost fix on thy mother eternal disgrace, and dost violate the inherited laws of mighty Sparta. But if thou dost perish by my hand, they will call me an unlucky mother, but saved from disgrace together with my country.”

poems.title: Book IX, 400
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Revered Hypatia, ornament of learning, stainless star of wise teaching, when I see thee and thy discourse I worship thee, looking on the starry house of the Virgin; for thy business is in heaven.

poems.title: Book IX, 401
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Nature, loving the duties of friendship, invented instruments by which absent friends can converse, pens, paper, ink, handwriting, tokens of the heart that mourns afar off.

poems.title: Book IX, 441: On a Statue of Heracles
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: I marvelled seeing at the cross-roads Jove’s brazen son, once constantly invoked, now cast aside, and in wrath I said: “Averter of woes, offspring of three nights, thou, who never didst suffer defeat, art to-day laid low.” But at night the god stood by my bed smiling, and said: “Even though I am a god I have learnt to serve the times.”

poems.title: Book IX, 484
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Odysseus once, when sailing on the sea, received as a gift a bag of winds—a very valuable thing. But this my Aeolus of the windy heart sends me a fowl stuffed with wind. You send me winged winds, my friend, yes wind, and I can’t eat compressed air.

poems.title: Book IX, 486
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: When my slave untied the paunch! you sent me, after tying it up yourself, he found it to be a bellows full of air.

poems.title: Book IX, 487
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: You served me the food of fig-fattened pigs from Cyprus, dry and thirst-provoking. But when you find me sufficiently fig-fattened, either kill me at once or quench my thirst with Cyprian wine.

poems.title: Book IX, 489
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: A grammarian’s daughter, having known a man, gave birth to a child which was masculine, feminine, and neuter. ;

poems.title: Book IX, 502
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: I require “conditum.”! Where did “conditum” get its name from for it is alien to the Greek - tongue. If it is a Latin word you will know, who are such a good Latin scholar. Prepare it for me, then, for the malady of the stomach from which I suffer requires this drink, I am told.

poems.title: Book IX, 503
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: I was not wrong in saying that there is a divine virtue in dzzyphi. The other day at least I applied a dizyphos to one suffering from a chronic quartan ague, and he became at once as fit as a dog-tick.

poems.title: Book IX, 508
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: If one wishes to enjoy a happy day, meeting you makes his day a good one; but if one wishes the contrary, not meeting you makes it a bad one:

poems.title: Book IX, 528: On the House of Marina
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: The inhabitants of Olympus, having become Christians, live here undisturbed; for here they shall not be put on the fire in the melting-pot that produces necessary small change.

poems.title: Book IX, 773
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: The smith transformed Love into a frying-pan, and not unreasonably, as it also burns.

poems.title: Book IX, 168
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: I, unhappy man, have married a wife who is “pernicious wrath,” and my profession, too, obliges me to begin with “wrath.” Oh, man of much wrath, forced to consort with wrath in two things, my calling as a grammarian and my combative wife!

poems.title: Book X, 32
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.note: Paton prints the name in square brackets (attribution doubtful).
poems.text: There’s many a slip ‘twixt the cup and the lip.

poems.title: Book X, 34
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: If concern avail aught, take thought and let things concern thee; but if God is concerned for thee, what does it concern thee? Without God thou shalt neither take thought nor be unconcerned ; but that aught concern thee is the concern of God.

poems.title: Book X, 44
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: If a friend receives a present he at once writes beginning “Lord brother,’ but if he gets nothing he only says “ Brother.” For these words are to be bought and sold. I at least wish no “Lord,” for I have nothing to give.

poems.title: Book X, 45
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: If thou rememberest, O man, how thy father sowed thee, thou shalt cease from thy proud thoughts. But dreaming Plato hath engendered pride in thee, calling thee immortal and a “heavenly plant.” “Of dust thou art made. Why dost thou think proudly?” So one might speak, clothing the fact in more grandiloquent fiction; but if thou seekest the truth, thou art sprung from incontinent lust and a filthy drop.

poems.title: Book X, 46
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Silence is men’s chief learning. The sage Pythagoras himself is my witness. He, knowing himself how to speak, taught others to be silent, having discovered this potent drug to ensure tranquillity.

poems.title: Book X, 47
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Eat and drink and keep silence in mourning ; for we should not, as Homer said, mourn the dead with our belly. Yes, and he shows us Niobe, who buried her twelve dead children all together, taking thought for food.

poems.title: Book X, 48
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: It is a proverb, that no woman who has been a slave should ever become a mistress. I will tell you something similar. ‘ Let no man who has been an advocate ever become a judge, not even if he be a greater orator than Isocrates. For how can a man who has served for hire in a fashion no more respectable than a whore judge a case otherwise than dirtily?”’

poems.title: Book X, 49
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: They say that even ants and gnats have bile. So, while the most insignificant beasts have bile, do you bid me have no bile and lie exposed to the attacks of all the world, not even wronging by mere words those who wrong me by deeds? I have for the rest of my life to stop up my mouth with a rush and not even breathe.

poems.title: Book X, 50
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: I deny that Circe, as Homer says, changed those who visited her from men into pigs or wolves. No she was a cunning courtesan, and made them who took her bait poorest of the poor. Stripping them of their human sense, she now, when they could gain nothing for themselves, reared them in her house like senseless animals. But Ulysses, having his wits about him and avoiding the folly of youth, possessed a counter-charm to enchantment, his own nature, not Hermes, emplanting reason in him.

poems.title: Book X, 51
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Envy, says Pindar, is better than pity. Those who are envied lead a splendid life, while our pity is for the excessively unfortunate. I would be neither too fortunate nor too badly off; for the mean is best, since the height of fortune is apt to bring danger, while the depth of misery exposes to insult.

poems.title: Book X, 52
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Well didst thou say it, right well, Menander, and like a true nursling of the Muses and Graces, that Opportunity is a god; for often a thought that occurs opportunely of itself finds something better than much reflection.

poems.title: Book X, 53
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: That we see murderers blest by fortune does not surprise me much. It is the gift of Zeus. For he would have killed his father, whom he hated, had Cronos chanced to be mortal. Now, instead of killing him, he punishes him in the same place as the Titans, casting him bound like a robber into the pit.

poems.title: Book X, 54
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Consumption is not the only cause of death, but extreme obesity often has the same result. Dionysius, tyrant of the Pontic Heraclea, testifies to this, for it is what befel him.

poems.title: Book X, 55
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: If you boast that you don’t in any way obey your wife’s orders, you are talking nonsense: for you are not made of tree or stone, as the saying is,' and you suffer what most or all of us suffer, you are ruled by a woman. But if you say, “She does not smack me with her slipper, nor have I an unchaste wife whom I must put up with and shut my eyes,’ I say your servitude is milder than that of others, as you have sold yourself to a chaste and not very severe mistress.

poems.title: Book X, 56
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: There is no manifest sign of chastity: this I tell husbands who are made fools of. Neither are ill-looks quite free from suspicion, nor is every pretty woman naturally vicious. For a woman may refuse to yield to those who are ready to pay a high price owing to her beauty, and we see many who are not good-looking never satisfied with amorous intercourse, and giving large presents to those who possess them. Nor if a woman is always frowning and is never seen to laugh, and avoids showing herself to men, is this behaviour a pledge of chastity. On the contrary, the most grave of them may turn out to be whores in secret, and the merry ones who are amiable to everyone may be virtuous, if any woman is entirely virtuous. Is age, then, a criterion? But not even old age has peace from the goad of Aphrodite. We trust then to oaths and her religious awe. But after her oath she can go and seek out twelve newer gods.

poems.title: Book X, 57
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: May God look with hatred on the belly and its food ; for it is owing to them that chastity breaks down.

poems.title: Book X, 58
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Naked I alighted on the earth and naked shall I go beneath it. Why do I toil in vain, seeing the end is nakedness ?

poems.title: Book X, 59
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: The expectation of death is a trouble full of pain, and a mortal, when he dies, gains freedom from this. Weep not then for him who departs from life, for there is no suffering beyond death.

poems.title: Book X, 60
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: You are wealthy. And what is the end of it? When you depart do you trail your riches after you as you are being pulled to your tomb? You gather wealth spending time, but you cannot pile up a heavier measure of life.

poems.title: Book X, 61
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Avoid the rich; they are shameless, domestic tyrants, hating poverty, the mother of temperance.

poems.title: Book X, 62
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Fortune knows neither reason nor law, but rules men despotically, carried along without reason by her own current. She is rather inclined to favour the wicked, and hates the just, as if making a display of her unreasoning force.

poems.title: Book X, 63
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: A poor man has never lived, and does not even die, for when he seemed to be alive the unfortunate wretch was like a corpse. But for those who enjoy great prosperity and much wealth death is the ruin of life.

poems.title: Book X, 65
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Life is a perilous voyage; for often we are tempest-tossed in it and are in a worse case than shipwrecked men. With Fortune at Life’s helm we sail uncertainly as on the open sea, some on a fair voyage, others the reverse: but all alike reach one harbour under the earth.

poems.title: Book X, 72
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: All life is a stage and a play: either learn to play laying your gravity aside, or bear with life’s pains.

poems.title: Book X, 73
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: If the gale of Fortune bear thee, bear with it and be borne; but if thou rebellest and tormentest thyself, even so the gale bears thee.

poems.title: Book X, 75
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: We live—all who live as this life is—and gaze on the flame of the sun, breathing through our nostrils delicate air; we are organs which receive health as a gift from the life-creating breezes. But if anyone with his hand presses tightly a little of our breath, he robs us of our life and brings us down to Hades. So being nothing we are fed with vanity, pasturing on air drawn from a breath of wind.

poems.title: Book X, 77
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Why dost thou labour in vain, O man, and disturb everything, being, as thou art, the slave of the lot that fell to thee at birth? Resign thyself to this, and struggle not against Fate, but content with thy fortune, love tranquillity. Yet strive thou rather, even against Fate, to lead thy delighted spirit to mirth.

poems.title: Book X, 78
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Cast away complaint and be not troubled, for how brief is the time thou dwellest here compared with all the life that follows this! Ere thou breedest worms and art cast into the tomb torment not thy soul, as if it were damned while thou still livest.

poems.title: Book X, 79
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: We are born day by day when night departs, retaining nothing of our former life, estranged from the doings of yesterday and beginning to-day the remainder of our life. Do not then, old man, say thy years are too many, for to-day thou hast no part in those that have gone by.

poems.title: Book X, 80
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: The life of men is the plaything of Fortune, a wretched life and a vagrant, tossed. between riches and poverty. Some whom she had cast down she casteth on high again like a ball, and others she brings down from the clouds to Hades.

poems.title: Book X, 81
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Alas for the brevity of life’s pleasure! Mourn the swiftness of time. We sit and we sleep, toiling or taking our delight, and time is advancing, advancing against us wretched men, bringing to each the end of life.

poems.title: Book X, 82
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Is it not true that we are dead and only seem to live, we Greeks, fallen into misfortune, fancying that a dream is life? Or are we alive and is life dead ?

poems.title: Book X, 83
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Even wisdom to the wealthy is a difficulty, a trouble, a necessity ....

poems.title: Book X, 84
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: In tears I was born and after tears I die, finding the whole of life a place of many tears. O race of men tearful, weak, pitiful, scarce seen on earth and straight dissolved !

poems.title: Book X, 85
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: We are all kept and fed for death, like a herd of swine to be slain without reason.

poems.title: Book X, 86
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: I Too rear, not sumptuously, but still I rear children, a wife, a slave, poultry and a dog—for no flatterer sets foot in my house.

poems.title: Book X, 87
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: If we do not laugh at life the runaway, and Fortune the strumpet shifting with the current, we cause ourselves constant pain seeing the unworthy luckier than ourselves.

poems.title: Book X, 88
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: The body is an affliction of the soul, it is Hell, Fate, a burden, a necessity, a strong chain and a tormenting punishment. But when the soul issues from the body as from the bonds of death, it flies to the immortal God.

poems.title: Book X, 89
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: If Rumour be a goddess, she too as well as the other gods is oath with ine Greeks and cozens them with deceptive words. Rumour, if any evil befall thee, at once is proved to be true, and often the rapidity of events anticipates her.

poems.title: Book X, 90
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Alas for the extreme malice of envy! A man hates the fortunate whom God loves. So senselessly are we led astray by envy ; so ready are we to be the slaves of folly. We Greeks are men reduced to ashes, having the buried hopes of the dead; for to-day everything is turned upside down.

poems.title: Book X, 91
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: He who detests a man whom God loves, is guilty ot the greatest folly, for he manifestly takes up arms against God himself, being gifted by envy with excessive spite. One should rather love him whom God loves.

poems.title: Book X, 92
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Since thou givest judgments and art a subtle speaker, I bring thee too this grave epigram of my nightingale worthy of one who speaks freely ; for he who sings of thee pours forth the praises of Justice.

poems.title: Book X, 93
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: It is better to endure even straitened Fortune rather than the arrogance of the wealthy.

poems.title: Book X, 94
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: I rank God is a philosopher too, as he does not wax wroth at once with blasphemy, but with the advance of time increases the punishment of wicked and miserable men.

poems.title: Book X, 95
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: I hate the man who is double-minded, kind in words, but a foe in his conduct.

poems.title: Book X, 96
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: When I think over things, observing the inopportune changes of life and the fickle current of unfair Fortune, how she makes the poor rich and deprives its possessors of wealth, then blinded in my own mind by the error I hate everything owing to the obscurity of all. For how shall I get the better of Fortune, who keeps on appearing in life from no one knows where, behaving like a harlot.

poems.title: Book X, 97
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Having lived a pound of years with toiling Grammar I am sent to Hell to be senator of the dead.

poems.title: Book X, 98
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Every uneducated man is wisest if he remains silent, hiding his speech like a disgraceful disease.

poems.title: Book X, 99
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: I often, Sextus, weighed on the balance your kindness and insolence, and finding your kindness much the lightest and your abusive speech ever sinking the scale, I abandoned your friendship, unable to support any longer your most dishonouring insults.

poems.title: Book XI, 54
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: The women mock me for being old, bidding me look at the wreck of my years in the mirror. But I, as I approach the end of my life, care not whether I have white hair or black, and with sweet-scented ointments and crowns of lovely flowers and wine I make heavy care to cease.

poems.title: Book XI, 55
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Give me to drink, that wine may scatter my troubles, warming again my chilled heart.

poems.title: Book XI, 62
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Death is a debt due by all men and no mortal knows if he shall be alive to-morrow. Take this well to heart, O man, and make thee merry, since thou possessest wine that is oblivion of death. Take joy too in Aphrodite whilst thou leadest this fleeting life, and give up all else to the control of Fortune.

poems.title: Book XI, 204
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: I was thunderstruck when I saw the rhetor Maurus, with a snout like an elephant, emitting a voice that murders one from lips weighing a pound each.

poems.title: Book XI, 255
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Snub-Nosed Memphis danced the parts of Daphne and Niobe, Daphne as if he were wooden, and Niobe as if he were of stone.

poems.title: Book XI, 263
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Menander, standing over the comedian Paulus in his sleep, said: “I never did you any harm, and you speak me ill.”

poems.title: Book XI, 280
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Better to be judged by Hegemon, the slayer of robbers, than to fall into the hands of the surgeon Gennadius. For he executes murderers in just hatred, but Gennadius takes a fee for sending you down to Hades.

poems.title: Book XI, 281
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.note: Paton’s heading: “On Magnus the Expert Physician”.
poems.text: When Magnus went down to Hades, Pluto trembled and said: “He has come to set the dead, too, on their legs.”

poems.title: Book XI, 283
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Many people say many things, but yet they cannot express in words all the currents of your vices. But there is one strange and incredible thing I marvelled at in you: how, while you were stealing, you had tears ready to hand. Coming from the land of Chalcis he deprived our city of brass, stealing and stealing with profitable tears.

poems.title: Book XI, 285
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: We marvelled at another strange, effeminate characteristic. He wept while stealing, pitying those he was robbing; he who, while robbing, observed ceremonial purity, and while thus affecting purity went on despoiling, a man with nothing clean about him, not even his person free of dirt. And consequently was ‘incapable of doing any mischief.

poems.title: Book XI, 286
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: “ Nothing is worse than a woman, even a good one”; and nothing is worse than a slave, even a good one. But still one requires necessary evils. Do you suppose a slave bears his master affection? A good slave would be he who broke both his legs.”

poems.title: Book XI, 287
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: He who is cursed with an ugly wife sees darkness when he lights the lamps in the evening.

poems.title: Book XI, 288
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: A barber and a tailor came to blows with each other, and soon the needles got the better of the razor.

poems.title: Book XI, 289
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: O sweetest ravishment of life! A money-lender, while marking down on his tablets the interest of years, died instantly in the space of a moment, still grasping his interest in his fingers.

poems.title: Book XI, 290
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: One holding in his fingers a reckoning counter for the fingers went by the counter-vote of death in double-quick time to Hades. The counter now lives bereaved of the reckoner, whose soul is rapidly driven from hence.

poems.title: Book XI, 291
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: What good do you do to the city by writing verses, getting so much gold for your slanders, selling iambic verses as a shopman sells oil?

poems.title: Book XI, 292
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.note: Paton’s heading: “On a certain Philosopher who became Prefect of Constantinople in the reign of Valentinian and Valens”.
poems.text: Thou, seated above the heavenly wheel, hast desired a silver wheel. Oh, infinite shame! Erst thou wast of higher station and hast straight become much lower. Ascend hither to the depths; for now thou hast descended to the heights.

poems.title: Book XI, 293
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: O.Olympius promised me a horse, but brought me a tail from which hung a horse at its last gasp.

poems.title: Book XI, 299
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Thou waxest wanton! What wonder? Does it distress me? No, I bear with thee. For the boldness of the wanton is their punishment.

poems.title: Book XI, 300
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Thou speakest much, O man, but in a little thou shalt be laid on the ground. Silence and while thou yet livest meditate on death.

poems.title: Book XI, 301
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: The Sun to men is the god of light, but if he too were insolent to them in his shining, they would not desire even light.

poems.title: Book XI, 302
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Thou hast not insulted me, but my poverty; but if Zeus dwelt on earth in poverty, he himself also would have suffered insult.

poems.title: Book XI, 303
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: If I am poor, what shall it harm me? Why dost thou hate me who do no wrong? This is the fault of Fortune, not a vice of character.

poems.title: Book XI, 304
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: All are cowards and braggarts and whatever other fault there may be among men, yet he who has reason does not expose his fault to his neighbour, but in his wisdom hides it within. But thy soul’s door is flung wide open, and it is evident to all when thou crouchest in terror or art too brazen.

poems.title: Book XI, 305
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Child of shamelessness, most ignorant of men, ‘nursling of folly, tell why dost thou hold thy head high, knowing nothing? Among the grammarians thou art the Platonist, and if anyone enquire as to Plato’s doctrines thou art again a grammarian. From one thing thou takest refuge in another, and thou neither knowest the Art of Grammar nor art thou a Platonist.

poems.title: Book XI, 306
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Though you leave Alexandria for Antioch, and after Syria land in Italy, no man in power will ever wed you. The fact is you always are fancying that some one will, and therefore skip from city to city.

poems.title: Book XI, 307
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Your son is called Eros and your wife Aphrodite, and so, blacksmith, it is quite fair you should have a lame leg.

poems.title: Book XI, 317
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Someone gave me a long-suffering donkey that moves backwards as much as forward ? their journey’s haven to those who ride on it; a donkey, the son of slowness, a labour, a delay, a dream,’ but first instead of last for those who are retiring.

poems.title: Book XI, 323
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Corakes (crows) and colakes (flatterers) are only distinguished by Rho and Lambda. Therefore a crow and a lick-spittle flatterer are the same thing. So, my good sir, beware of this beast, knowing that flatterers are crows that pick the living too.

poems.title: Book XI, 340
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: I swore ten thousand times to make no more epigrams, for I had brought on my head the enmity of many fools, but when I set eyes on the face of the Paphlagonian Pentagathus I can’t repress the malady.

poems.title: Book XI, 341
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: It is best to praise, and blaming is the cause of enmity, but yet to speak ill of others is Attic honey.

poems.title: Book XI, 349
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Tell me whence comes it that thou measurest the Universe and the limits of the Earth, thou who bearest a little body made of a little earth ? Count thyself first and know thyself, and then shalt thou count this infinite Earth. And if thou canst not reckon thy body’s little store of clay, how canst thou know the measures of the immeasurable ?

poems.title: Book XI, 351
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: I let the cell yesterday to a barley-water maker, and to-day I found a formidable pugilist in it. And when I said, “Who art thou? Whence didst thou invade my house?” he up with his hands to box with me. I went off at the double, afraid of the savage man, on seeing the brewer suddenly turned into a bruiser. But by the boxer Pollux and Castor himself, and Zeus who hearkens to suppliants, keep the boxer, my aversion, off me; for I can’t have a stand-up fight at the beginning of every month.

poems.title: Book XI, 353
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Hermotycus’ daughter slept with a great ape and she gave birth to many little ape-Hermeses. If Zeus, transformed into a swan, got him from Leda Helen, Castor, and Pollux, with Hermione at least a crow lay, and, poor woman, she gave birth to a Hermes-crowd of horrible demons.”

poems.title: Book XI, 355
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: You say “I know all things,’ but you are imperfect in all things. ‘Tasting of everything, you have nothing that is your own.

poems.title: Book XI, 357
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: A son and father started a competitive contest as to which could eat up all the property by spending most, and after devouring absolutely all the money they have at last each other to eat up.

poems.title: Book XI, 371
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Do not invite me to witness your hunger-laden dishes, bringing me pumpkin pie to feast on. We don’t eat the solid silver you set before us, defrauding with famine fare the poor trenchers. Seek those who are keeping their fast for your display of silver, and then you will be admired for your lightly loaded plate.

poems.title: Book XI, 373
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.note: Paton’s heading: “On a Poet playing at Dice”.
poems.text: Calliope is the goddess of all poets: your Calliope is called Tabliope.

poems.title: Book XI, 377
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: We guests had a miserable fowl to eat and were ourselves devoured by other birds. Two vultures eat Tityus under earth and four vultures eat us alive.

poems.title: Book XI, 378
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: I cannot put up with a wife and with Grammar too, Grammar that is penniless and a wife who is injurious. What I suffer from both is Death and Fate. Now I have just with difficulty escaped from Grammar, but I cannot escape from this shrewish wife, for our contract and Roman law prevent it.

poems.title: Book XI, 381
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Every woman is a source of annoyance, but she has two good seasons, the one in her bridal chamber and the other when she is dead.

poems.title: Book XI, 383
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: So for mokes, too, there is sinister and good Fortune, and Saturn rules the nativities of beasts also; for ever since evil time befel this donkey, it has become a grammarian’s instead of being in the alabarch’s palace. But bear it patiently henceforth, donkey; for grammarians crithe (barley) has no end, but is called only cri.

poems.title: Book XI, 384
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: If solitaries (monks), why so many? And if so many, how again are they solitary? O crowd of solitaries who give the lie to solitude!

poems.title: Book XI, 385
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Thy love is counterfeit and thou lovest from fear and by force. But nothing is more treacherous than such love.

poems.title: Book XI, 386
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Yesterday a certain man seeing Victory in town sour-faced, said: “Goddess Victory, what has befallen thee, then?” But she, lamenting and finding fault with the decision, said: “ Dost thou alone not know it? I have been given to Patricius.” So Victory, too, was in deep grief at being illegally caught by the sailor Patricius as if she were a breeze.

poems.title: Book XI, 387
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Everyone takes but one meal, but when Salaminus feasts us we go home and breakfast a second time.

poems.title: Book XV, 20
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Pass by this miserable life in silence, imitating by thy silence Time himself. Live likewise unnoticed; or if not, thou shalt be so in death.

poems.title: Book XVI, 207: On a Statue of Love
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Love is unarmed; therefore he smiles and is gentle, for he has not his bow and fiery arrows. And it is not without reason that he holds in his hands a dolphin and a flower, for in one he holds the earth, in the other the sea.

poems.title: Book XVI, 282
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Here we are, the Victories, the laughing maidens, bringing victories to the city that loveth righteousness. Those to whom the city is dear painted us, fashioning us in such forms as are proper to Victories.

poems.title: Book XVI, 284: On another Picture of a Dancing Girl in the Sosthenion
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: I am Helladia of Byzantium, and here I stand where the people in spring celebrate the dance, here where the land is divided by the strait; for both continents praised my dancing.

poems.title: Book XVI, 285: On the Gilded Picture of a Female Lyrist
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: No one put gold on Anthusa, but the son of Cronos poured himself on her, as once on Danae. But he did not come near her body, for his mind was seized with shame, lest against his will he should consort with one of the Muses.

poems.title: Book XVI, 286: On the Dancer Helladia
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: The feminine nature excels in dancing: give way, young men! The Muse and Helladia laid down this law, the one because she first invented the rhythm of movement, the other because she reached perfection in the art.

poems.title: Book XVI, 287: On the Same
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.text: Someone sang the lay of Hector, a new tune, and Helladia, donning a chlamys, accompanied the melody. In the dancing of this goddess of war there was both desire and terror, for with virile strength she mingled feminine grace.

poems.title: Fortune's Master (Mackail)
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: No more is Hope or Fortune my concern, nor for what remains do I reck of your deceit; I have reached harbour. I am a poor man, but living in Freedom's company I turn my face away from wealth the scorner of poverty.

poems.title: The Married Man (Mackail)
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: If you boast high that you are not obedient to your wife's commands, you talk idly, for you are not sprung of oak or rock, as the saying is; and, as is the hard case with most or all of us, you too are in woman's rule. But if you say, "I am not struck with a slipper, nor my wife being unchaste have I to bear it and shut my eyes," I reply that your bondage is lighter, in that you have sold yourself to a reasonable and not to too hard a mistress.

poems.title: The Faultless Dancer (Mackail)
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Snub-nosed Memphis danced Daphnis and Niobe; Daphne like a stock, Niobe like a stone.

poems.title: Minimum Credula Postero (Mackail)
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: All human must pay the debt of death, nor is there any mortal who knows whether he shall be alive to-morrow; learning this clearly, O man, make thee merry, keeping the wine-god close by thee for oblivion of death, and take thy pleasure with the Paphian while thou drawest thy ephemeral life; but all else give to Fortune's control.

poems.title: Parta Quies (Mackail)
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Expectation of death is woful grief, and this is the gain of a mortal when he perishes; weep not then for him who departs from life, for after death there is no other accident.

poems.title: The Voyage of Life (Mackail)
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Life is a dangerous voyage; for tempest-tossed in it we often strike rocks more pitiably than shipwrecked men; and having Chance as pilot of life, we sail doubtfully as on the sea, some on a fair voyage, and others contrariwise; yet all alike we put into the one anchorage under earth.

poems.title: Daily Birth (Mackail)
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Day by day we are born as night retires, no more possessing aught of our former life, estranged from our course of yesterday, and beginning to-day the life that remains. Do not then call thyself, old man, abundant in years; for to-day thou hast no share in what is gone.

poems.title: The Breath of Life (Mackail)
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Breathing thin air into our nostrils we live and look on the torch of the sun, all we who live what is called life; and are as organs, receiving our spirits from quickening airs. If one then chokes that little breath with his hand, he robs us of life, and brings us down to Hades. Thus being nothing we wax high in hardihood, feeding on air from a little breath.

poems.title: The Price of Riches (Mackail)
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Thou art rich, and what of it in the end? as thou departest, dost thou drag thy riches with thee, pulling them into the coffin? Thou gatherest riches at expense of time, and thou canst not heap up more exceeding measures of life.

poems.title: Nil Expedit (Mackail)
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Naked I came on earth, and naked I depart under earth, and why do I vainly labour, seeing the naked end?

poems.title: The Slaughter-House (Mackail)
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: We all are watched and fed for Death as a herd of swine butchered wantonly.

poems.title: Lacrimae Rerum (Mackail)
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Weeping I was born and having wept I die, and I found all my living amid many tears. O tearful, weak, pitiable race of men, dragged under earth and mouldering away!

poems.title: Quietism (Mackail)
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Why vainly, O man, dost thou labour and disturb everything when thou art slave to the lot of thy birth? Yield thyself to it, strive not with Heaven, and, accepting thy fortune, be content with rest.

poems.title: Equanimity (Mackail)
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: If that which bears all things bears thee, bear thou and be borne; and if thou art indignant and vexest thyself, even so that which bears all things bears thee.

poems.title: The Rules of the Game (Mackail)
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: All life is a stage and a game: either learn to play it, laying by seriousness, or bear its pains.

poems.title: The Last Word (Mackail)
poems.author: Palladas of Alexandria
poems.collection: Select Epigrams from the Greek Anthology (1890)
poems.text: Thou talkest much, O man, and thou art laid in earth after a little: keep silence, and while thou yet livest, meditate on death.
